lessons.title: The 5 Ws and H
lessons.tip: A news story answers six questions: Who? What? Where? When? Why? and How? Reporters check that every story answers them. If an answer is missing, ask another question.
sources: Common newsroom conventions: the 5 Ws and H, the inverted pyramid, attribution (concepts only)
Society of Professional Journalists, Code of Ethics (accuracy and fairness; summarized, not quoted)

lessons.title: Open and closed questions
lessons.tip: A closed question has a short answer, such as yes or no. An open question starts with words like what, how or why and invites a longer answer. Reporters use open questions to get stories and closed questions to check facts.

lessons.title: Follow-up questions
lessons.tip: A follow-up question builds on what the person just said. It shows you listened, and it gets details. Good follow-ups are “Can you give an example?”, “What happened next?” and “Why was that important?”

lessons.title: The inverted pyramid
lessons.tip: News stories put the most important facts first and the smaller details later. The shape is an upside-down pyramid: wide at the top with the key facts, and narrow at the bottom with extra details. If a reader stops after the first paragraph, they still know the story.
sources: Common newsroom conventions: the 5 Ws and H, the inverted pyramid, attribution (concepts only)
Society of Professional Journalists, Code of Ethics (accuracy and fairness; summarized, not quoted)

lessons.title: Headlines and ledes
lessons.tip: A headline is a short title that tells the main news. It uses short, strong words and often drops small words like “the” and “a.” The lede is the first sentence of the story. It gives the most important facts clearly in one sentence.

lessons.title: Fact, opinion and doubt
lessons.tip: Reporters separate what is known from what is thought. A fact can be checked. An opinion is a view. When the facts are not sure, use careful words such as “police said,” “may have” and “according to.” Never state a guess as a fact.

lessons.title: Check facts with two sources
lessons.tip: A claim is stronger when two independent sources support it. Independent means they did not get the information from each other. Ask where a source got the facts: did they see it, or hear it from someone else? Say how you know: “according to the police report” or “said two witnesses.” If you cannot confirm a detail, leave it out or say it is unconfirmed.

lessons.title: On the record, off the record
lessons.tip: Tell sources how you will use what they say. On the record means you can quote them by name. Background means you can use the information but not the name. Off the record means you cannot publish it. Agree on the rule before the information is shared, not after. Naming a person is usually best because readers can judge the source; use an anonymous source only when there is a real risk and a good reason.
sources: Public-domain style and ethics guidance for reporters (concepts only; no text copied)
Standard newsroom practice for attribution, balance and corrections (ideas only; original wording)

lessons.title: Report numbers with context
lessons.tip: A number alone says little. Add a comparison, a base and a source. “Robberies fell from 40 to 30” becomes clearer with “in a city of 200,000,” and a trend over time. Say percent when the base is clear: a fall from 40 to 30 is 25 percent. Round when exactness does not matter: “about 200,000.” Never report a small change as a large trend.

Standard newsroom practice for attribution, balance and corrections (ideas only; original wording)

lessons.title: Be fair and balanced
lessons.tip: Fair stories give the people involved a chance to respond. If you report a criticism, ask the person criticized for their side before you publish. Use neutral verbs: “said” is fairer than “claimed,” which suggests doubt. Do not use loaded words, such as “disaster” or “miracle,” unless a source says them. Balance does not mean pretending two unequal sides are equal; give more weight to the stronger evidence.
sources: Public-domain style and ethics guidance for reporters (concepts only; no text copied)
Standard newsroom practice for attribution, balance and corrections (ideas only; original wording)

lessons.title: Ethics: harm, privacy and conflicts
lessons.tip: Journalists balance the public’s right to know against possible harm. Ask: Is there a public interest, not just curiosity? lessons.title: Truth, opinion and fair comment
lessons.tip: Accuracy protects readers and the writer. A statement of fact that is true and well sourced is the strongest position. Opinion is different: label it clearly and base it on stated facts. Be careful with serious allegations: have documents or two reliable sources, offer the person a chance to respond, and report their reply. When you report a statement from an official source or court, attribute it precisely. Corrections should be prominent and prompt. This is not legal advice; follow your editor’s guidance.
